overview.intro: The numbers of the product's admin dashboard, read from the product database through the console's read-only connection when you refresh a panel.

health.intro: The worker's job queue, the pods of this environment and their logs: what used to need kubectl. Each panel is the result of its last refresh; nothing here refreshes on its own.

def.queue: Queue: every job by kind and status. The table keeps finished jobs too.
def.oldest: Oldest queued: how long the oldest job still waiting for a worker has waited. Minutes is normal after an upload; hours means no worker is claiming.
def.stale: Stale claim: a running job whose lock is older than {minutes} minutes. Its worker died; the next poll puts it back in the queue, or fails it when its attempts are used up.
def.loop: Retry loop: a job claimed twice or more that is still queued or running - a worker killed in the middle of it, again and again (out of memory). After {attempts} attempts the job fails.
def.failed: Failed (24 h): jobs that ended failed in the last 24 hours. Last failures lists the newest 20 with the worker's error.

pods.title: Pods
pods.noMetrics: This cluster reports no memory use (no metrics-server); limits are still shown.

def.restarts: Restarts: how often the container restarted since its pod was created. A deploy replaces the pod and starts the count again.
def.last: Last termination: why the container's previous run ended (OOMKilled is out of memory), its exit code and when. Kubernetes keeps only the last one.
def.restarted: Restarted (24 h): containers whose last termination was in the last 24 hours. Kubernetes keeps no history of restarts, so this counts containers, not restarts: a worker killed 900 times is one container with 900 restarts.
def.memory: Memory: what the container uses now, against its limit. Near the limit (red past 90%) is where the out-of-memory killer acts.
def.events: Events: the newest the cluster still keeps, about an hour: scheduling, failing probes, back-off, kills.

logs.title: Logs
logs.intro: Read when you ask, never stored by the console: logs can carry emails and ids. Each read is recorded in the console's audit with your name and filter.
